resources.string: Kanako takes one screenshot when you tap the floating control, or after detected changes settle if you enable auto-read, to generate furigana on your device. Images are held in memory during recognition, then discarded; they are not saved or uploaded. Window, scroll, keyboard, and password metadata clears outdated annotations and blocks capture around sensitive input. Kanako does not read text from input fields through accessibility.

Enable Kanako in Android Accessibility settings to use tap-to-read. Each reading request takes one screenshot of the current app on Android 14 or later, or the display on Android 11–13. Reading starts with a tap unless you separately enable auto-read in Preferences. Recognition runs on your device. Images are held in memory during recognition, then discarded; they are not saved or uploaded.

Kanako uses window, scroll, keyboard, and password metadata to clear old annotations and block capture around sensitive input. It does not read input-field text through accessibility. Screen images can still contain private information, so read only content you want Kanako to process.

There is no continuous screen-sharing session. You can stop the floating control or disable the accessibility service at any time.

Swipe down twice to open Quick Settings. Tap Edit, then drag the Kanako tile into your active tiles. Tap it to show or stop the floating reader. Adding the tile does not take a screenshot. Starting the reader schedules a reading if Auto-read is enabled.
Auto-read waits for changes to settle. Tap to read gives you control.

While the floating reader is active, Kanako will automatically take a screenshot after scrolling, app changes, or content updates settle for about 0.7 seconds. It also reads when the reader starts or the device is unlocked. No tap is needed. Images are processed locally in memory, then discarded; they are not saved or uploaded.\n\nThis uses individual screenshots, not a recording session. Capture is blocked around detected sensitive input and on the lock screen. Stability and scroll tracking depend on events from the source app; animations may not be detected. You can turn this option off at any time.

Choose a topic for quick answers and guidance.
Kanako takes one screenshot, recognizes Japanese on your device, and places readings over the current view. Tap again to clear. Double tap or hold for controls.
Move on when you are ready

Readings follow scrolling reported by the source app. Uncertain movement clears them. Optional Auto-read reads after detected changes settle for about 0.7 seconds, and after reader start or unlock. Tracking depends on the source app.

Screen images are processed in memory, then discarded without saving or uploading. Capture is blocked around detected sensitive input and on the lock screen. Camera photos also remain temporary unless you explicitly choose Save with furigana.

Kanji recognition and readings are not always correct. Similar-looking kanji and katakana can be confused; names and words with several readings can also be misread. Small, stylized, blurry text and mixed layouts make recognition harder. Furigana positions are estimated from the recognized text. Protected screens cannot be captured.
Japanese recognition may need an initial model download through Google Play services. Once available, recognition runs on your device. Each reading request uses processing power.

Swipe down twice, tap Edit, then add Kanako to your active tiles. Tap it to show or stop the floating reader. Adding the tile does not capture a screenshot. Missing access opens Home. With Auto-read enabled, starting the reader also schedules a reading.

Open Camera from Home; its permission is separate from screen reading access. Read live, or capture a photo for stable reading. Tap a reading or its kanji to bring that reading in front; tap overlapping readings again to cycle through them. Tap elsewhere in the live view to focus. Pinch to zoom; on a photo, drag to move and double tap to reset. Save with furigana exports the whole photo with the selected reading in front, regardless of your current zoom.

Choose Kana or Romaji, reading size, color, and plates in Preferences. With Touch through readings on, you can use the app underneath the furigana. Turn it off to tap a reading or its kanji and bring that reading in front; tap overlapping readings again to cycle through them. Hide button while typing hides the mascot when the keyboard is visible. Capture pauses while a keyboard or password field is detected, even when the mascot stays visible. The fixed preview shows appearance only.
Applies to both readers. The preview shows appearance only.

On Home, set up display-over-apps and screen reading access after reviewing the disclosure. Choose Show floating reader, then open Japanese content in another app. Screen reading needs Android 11 or later.
Drag the character to move it. Hold it to open controls and choose Stop floating reader. You can also stop it from Home or the notification.

Each screen reading takes one screenshot: the current app on Android 14 or later, or the display on Android 11–13. Window, scroll, keyboard, and password metadata clears old readings and blocks capture around detected sensitive input and on the lock screen. Input-field text is not collected through accessibility. Auto-read requires separate agreement and can be turned off in Preferences.

Check screen access on Home. If the service is connecting, wait or turn Kanako off and on in Android Accessibility settings. For a missing recognition model, connect to the internet and retry. In Camera, try focusing, moving closer, or capturing a photo. Tap the floating character to clear readings that no longer line up.
Read printed Japanese with your camera. No screen reading access needed.
Two access settings are needed for the floating reader.
Open another app, then tap Kanako to read. With Auto-read enabled, reading starts after detected changes settle.
